Short case 17 · General Surgery

Hydrocele

Three signs make the diagnosis: you can get above it, it transilluminates, and you cannot feel the testis separately. Then one question decides the management: is it primary, or is the testis underneath it diseased?

S Das: clinical method Bailey & Love: mechanism and management SRB: exam framework

1Definition and types

Definition
B&L: "A hydrocele is an abnormal collection of serous fluid in a part of the processus vaginalis, usually the tunica vaginalis around the testis and occasionally along the spermatic cord."​B&L 86 · p.1564 SRB: the collection of fluid between the two layers of the tunica.​SRB 26 · p.1057
Incidence, and the newborn figure that explains everything
Hydroceles affect an estimated 1% of adult men. More than 80% of newborn boys have a patent processus vaginalis, but most close spontaneously,​B&L 86 · p.1564 with closure beginning in late gestation and continuing through infancy and childhood.​B&L 86 · p.1564 That is why a congenital hydrocele in an infant is usually watched, and why one in an adult is not.
B&L's three structural types
1. Communicating or congenital: a patent processus vaginalis permits flow of peritoneal fluid into the tunica vaginalis, and it is associated with indirect inguinal hernias. 2. Non-communicating or vaginal: the processus is closed, with no communication with the peritoneal cavity; fluid accumulates from excessive production or defective absorption. 3. And the cord variety, where the collection lies along the spermatic cord.​B&L 86 · p.1564
SRB's four anatomical types, which is the Indian exam answer
Vaginal hydrocele: around the testis, the commonest. Infantile hydrocele: the tunica and processus are distended up to the internal ring, but the sac has no connection with the peritoneal cavity. SRB's own wording. Note the consequence: this is the one hydrocele you cannot always get above. Congenital hydrocele: communicates with the peritoneal cavity through a patent processus at the internal ring. Encysted hydrocele of the cord: a localised collection along the cord.​SRB 26 · p.1057
How to keep them straightWork from the internal ring down: congenital reaches the peritoneum, infantile reaches the internal ring but is shut off from it, vaginal is confined to the tunica, encysted is an isolated pocket on the cord.
And primary versus secondary
B&L: acquired hydroceles are primary or idiopathic, or secondary to epididymal or testicular disease.​B&L 86 · p.1564 That distinction is the whole management question.
The fluid, and the detail that explains a clinical fact SRB: hydrocele fluid is amber-coloured with a specific gravity of 1.022 to 1.024, and contains water, salts, albumin and fibrinogen. Then the sentence worth memorising: "Per se, hydrocele fluid does not clot, but if it comes in contact with the blood, fibrinogen gets activated and clots firmly." It often contains cholesterol and tyrosine crystals.​SRB 26 · p.1057

So: aspirate a hydrocele and the fluid stays liquid; aspirate it traumatically and the blood in it makes it clot, which is why repeated aspiration gives you a thick-walled, loculated sac that is harder to operate on later.
Aetiology of a primary hydrocele
SRB's four mechanisms: defective absorption of fluid by the tunica vaginalis, probably from damage to the endothelial wall by low-grade infection; excessive production, as in a secondary hydrocele; interference with drainage of fluid; and a patent processus.​SRB 26 · p.1057

2Examination: the three signs, and the fourth that matters most

Before you touch the patient The examiner is marking this before you have found anything. Bailey & Love gives it as a sequence: "ensure you have followed appropriate hand hygiene guidance. Introduce yourself and check the patient's name and date of birth. Request presence of a chaperone as appropriate. Explain what you are going to do, obtain verbal consent and ensure that the patient is comfortable."​B&L 35 · p.472 And the standard it is held to: "patients should be treated with respect and dignity, receive a clear explanation of the examination undertaken and be kept as comfortable as possible. A chaperone should be present, especially for intimate examinations."​B&L 21 · p.285

Do it, and be heard doing itWash your hands. Introduce yourself. Say what you want to examine and why, and ask permission. Ask for a chaperone where the examination is intimate. Expose what you need and cover the rest. Warm your hands. Tell the patient what each step will feel like and that they can ask you to stop, examine the tender part last, and watch their face rather than only your hands. Cover them and thank them before you turn to the examiner.

This one is intimate, so the chaperone is not a courtesy B&L's wording is "especially for intimate examinations", and it adds that this "should be part of a local guideline or policy".​B&L 21 · p.285 Offer a chaperone whatever your sex and the patient's, say that you have offered, and say you would record it. For a child, explain it to the child and ask the parent. If consent is refused, say that you would explain again, offer a chaperone, document the refusal, and not proceed. Examiners ask what you would do if she declined, and that is the whole answer.
1. Can you get above it?
Yes in a hydrocele: it is a purely scrotal swelling, and above it you feel only normal cord. No in an inguinoscrotal hernia, where the swelling is continuous with the canal.​Das 38 · p.597–598 This is the first and most important manoeuvre, because it separates hydrocele from hernia before anything else.
2. Does it transilluminate?
Yes, in a darkened room with a torch applied to one side. A clear fluid-filled sac glows. It will not transilluminate if the sac is thick-walled, if the fluid is blood (haematocele) or pus (pyocele), or if the swelling is solid.
3. Is it fluctuant, and can you feel the testis?
Fluctuant, and in a vaginal hydrocele the testis is not palpable separately because the fluid surrounds it. In an epididymal cyst you can feel the testis separately, below and in front. That is the cleanest distinction between the two commonest scrotal cysts.
4. Is the testis normal? The question that matters most
Because a secondary hydrocele is secondary to epididymal or testicular disease,​B&L 86 · p.1564 and the diseases in question are tuberculous epididymo-orchitis and testicular tumour. In a tense primary hydrocele you cannot palpate the testis, which is exactly why you must image it.
SoEvery hydrocele in an adult needs an ultrasound of the testis. That is the single most important sentence in this case.
Primary versus secondary, at the bedside Primary: large, often tense, testis impalpable within it, no pain, long history.
Secondary: usually small and lax, so the testis is palpable and the underlying disease can be felt; often with pain, or a history of fever, trauma or weight loss.

The rule of thumb is counter-intuitive and therefore examinable: a big tense hydrocele is usually primary and benign; a small lax hydrocele is the one hiding a tumour. And in either case, the ultrasound decides.
But learn the exception with the rule, because here it is the commoner caseSRB states both in consecutive sentences. The secondary hydrocele "is usually small, lax and testis is usually palpable (unlike primary hydrocele). Exception is, secondary hydrocele due to filariasis. It can be very large."​SRB 26 · p.1059 The chylocele is the same story: it "usually occurs after repeated attacks of filarial epididymitis" and "hydrocele is usually of large size and the sac is thickened".​SRB 26 · p.1059
In India that exception is not a curiosity, it is most of them, because B&L puts filarial hydroceles and chyloceles at up to 80% of hydroceles in tropical countries.​B&L 86 · p.1566 So a big tense hydrocele in this practice is as likely to be a secondary filarial one as a primary one, and the rule of thumb settles nothing by itself. That is why the ultrasound sentence above is the one that matters.

SRB's chapter sets the differentials out together: haematocele, pyocele, cyst of epididymis, spermatocele, varicocele, and primary and secondary vaginal hydrocele.​SRB 26 · p.1056

3Investigations

Ultrasound of the scrotum
To confirm the fluid, and more importantly to see the testis you cannot palpate.​B&L 86 · p.1565 Non-negotiable in an adult, and particularly in a young adult, because a testicular tumour can present as a hydrocele.
Tumour markers if the ultrasound is abnormal
Alpha-fetoprotein, beta-human chorionic gonadotrophin and lactate dehydrogenase, before any intervention.
And look for the cause of a secondary hydrocele
In India this is the commonest answer by a wide margin, and B&L gives it a section of its own: "filarial hydroceles and chyloceles account for up to 80% of hydroceles in tropical countries, where the parasite Wuchereria bancrofti is endemic. Filarial hydroceles follow repeated attacks of filarial epididymo-orchitis... In longstanding chyloceles, there are dense adhesions between the scrotum and its contents. Filarial elephantiasis supervenes in a small number of cases."​B&L 86 · p.1566
Eighty per cent is the number to carryIn a tropical practice the filarial hydrocele is not a footnote to the primary one, it is the usual one. B&L also notes the fluid may contain microfilariae, and it has its own treatment, which is the exception in the aspiration box below. And still consider tuberculous epididymo-orchitis, which gives a craggy, non-tender epididymis and sometimes a beaded vas.

4Treatment

In an infant
Observe. More than 80% of newborn boys have a patent processus vaginalis but most close spontaneously,​B&L 86 · p.1564 so a congenital hydrocele usually resolves. If it persists beyond about two years, or if there is a hernia, operate: herniotomy with ligation of the patent processus, approached through the groin rather than the scrotum.
In an adult: the operations, and what decides between them
B&L: "Established acquired hydroceles often have thick walls. There are three main surgical techniques for hydroceles."​B&L 86 · p.1565
1. Plication, Lord's operation, which is "suitable when the sac is reasonably thin walled". The sac is not excised or everted; it is bunched up with a series of sutures, so there is minimal dissection and the risk of haematoma is reduced.​B&L 86 · p.1565 That is the whole argument for it: the less tunica you raw-surface, the less there is to bleed.
2. Eversion. "The sac is opened and everted behind the testis, with placement of the testis in a pouch prepared by dissection in the fascial planes of the scrotum."​B&L 86 · p.1565 Used for a thicker sac, because a thick sac will not bunch. B&L warns that the cut edge bleeds, and that overrunning stitches at the cut edge can be used to reduce the risk of scrotal haematoma.​B&L 86 · p.1566
3. Aspiration, which B&L counts as the third technique rather than as a non-operation. See the amber box below, because the books take different lines on it.
And one more, from SRBSubtotal excision of the sac, for a thick sac, a large hydrocele or a chylocele. SRB explains why it is subtotal: "as tunica vaginalis is reflected on to the cord structures and epididymis posteriorly, total excision leads to orchidectomy with division of the cord."​SRB 26 · p.1060 That sentence is the one to remember. It is the anatomical reason a surgeon never tries to take the sac out whole.
The ruleThin sac, plicate. Thick sac, evert or partly excise. Being able to say what decides between them, the thickness of the sac, is worth more than the eponyms.
For a secondary hydrocele
Treat the cause. Draining the fluid without addressing a tuberculous epididymitis or a tumour achieves nothing and, in the case of a tumour, is harmful.
What exactly is Jaboulay's operation? The two books attach the name to different procedures A live disagreement about naming, and the one most likely to trip you in viva. B&L 86 p.1565 and SRB 26 pp.1059, 1060
Bailey & Love
Lists eversion as technique 2 and attaches the eponym to the pouch: the sac is opened and everted behind the testis, "with placement of the testis in a pouch prepared by dissection in the fascial planes of the scrotum (Jaboulay's procedure)".​B&L 86 · p.1565 On this reading, eversion plus a scrotal pouch is Jaboulay's.
SRB
Splits the two apart and gives them different names. Plain evacuation and eversion of the sac behind the testis is one option; "often the sac is excised partially and then eversion is done, which is called as Jaboulay's operation"; and placing the sac with the testis "in a newly created pocket between the fascial layers of the scrotum" is Sharma and Jhawer's technique.​SRB 26 · p.1060 SRB's own list of operations is accordingly five long: subtotal excision, Jaboulay's, evacuation and eversion, Lord's plication, Sharma and Jhawer's.​SRB 26 · p.1059 The name Sharma and Jhawer does not appear anywhere in B&L's testis and scrotum chapter.
Why they drifted apart
All three manoeuvres start the same way, by opening and everting the sac, and differ only in what is done afterwards: nothing, trim the redundant sac, or tuck the testis into a dartos pouch. Jaboulay described an eversion, and each book has attached his name to a different point on that spectrum. Neither is a misprint, and neither book acknowledges the other's usage.
How to answer: describe the operation, then name it, and say which book you are following. "I would open and evert the sac behind the testis. If the sac is redundant I would trim it first and then evert, which SRB calls Jaboulay's operation. Bailey and Love uses the name Jaboulay for eversion with the testis placed in a scrotal pouch, which SRB calls Sharma and Jhawer's technique." Any examiner will accept that, because it shows you know the step that matters and that the eponym is unsettled. For an Indian final-year paper, write SRB's five operations, since that is the list the question expects. Never lead with the eponym alone: say what you would do to the sac.
Has aspiration any place at all, or none? B&L 86 pp.1565, 1566 lists it as one of three techniques; SRB 26 p.1060 says it must be avoided
Bailey & Love
Counts it among the "three main surgical techniques" and gives it a defined indication: "Aspiration of the hydrocele fluid is simple, but the fluid always reaccumulates within a week or so. It may be suitable for men who are unfit for scrotal surgery, although hydrocele surgery can be undertaken under local anaesthetic."​B&L 86 · p.1566 It adds the risk, "aspiration can result in bleeding into the hydrocele sac and haematocele formation", and one extra option: "injection of a sclerosant, such as tetracycline, can be effective but painful."​B&L 86 · p.1566
SRB
"Aspiration must be avoided as much as possible as it is only a temporary measure (recurrence occurs very early) and chances of haematocele, infection are higher."​SRB 26 · p.1060 No indication is offered.
They agree on the facts and differ on the verdict
Both say it recurs and both say it can cause a haematocele. B&L then undercuts its own indication by pointing out that the definitive operation can be done under local anaesthetic, which removes most of the reason to aspirate an unfit man in the first place. So the difference is one of emphasis, not of evidence.
The filarial hydrocele, where the two books contradict each other outright
B&L makes aspiration the treatment: "treatment is by rest and aspiration with chronic cases treated by excision of the sac."​B&L 86 · p.1566 The same page puts filarial hydroceles and chyloceles at up to 80% of hydroceles in tropical countries, so this is not a footnote in India.
SRB says the opposite for exactly these hydrocelesIts prohibition is general — "aspiration must be avoided as much as possible" — and the operation it names for this group is the other one: "if the sac is thick, in large hydrocele and chylocele, subtotal excision of the sac is done."​SRB 26 · p.1060 The thick sac and the chylocele are the filarial hydrocele, which SRB describes a page earlier as following "repeated attacks of filarial epididymitis" with a sac that is "thickened".​SRB 26 · p.1059 So the books disagree about the same patient; this is not an exception one book grants.
And a prohibition from B&L that outranks both "If a tumour is suspected, the hydrocele should not be punctured (risk of malignant needle-track implantation)."​B&L 86 · p.1564 That is the mechanism behind the "never before excluding a tumour" clause in the ruling, and it is the sentence to quote, because it gives the reason rather than the rule.
Where that leaves youDo not offer aspiration as the treatment of a filarial hydrocele. Quote B&L's sentence if you are asked what the book says, and add in the same breath that SRB would excise a thick sac or a chylocele, and that nothing is punctured until a tumour has been excluded.
Outside the three books, flagged as such: current filarial morbidity management treats an established hydrocele surgically rather than by aspiration, and a thickened adherent sac refills almost at once after puncture. That is not in S Das, Bailey & Love or SRB, so do not lead with it, but it is why SRB's line is the safer of the two to act on.
How to answer: take SRB's line, then give B&L's two exceptions. "Aspiration is not a treatment for a primary vaginal hydrocele. It recurs within a week, it risks a haematocele, and repeated aspiration leaves a thickened loculated sac that is harder to operate on later. I would use it only for palliation in a man genuinely unfit for even a local-anaesthetic procedure, and never before excluding an underlying testicular tumour. On the filarial hydrocele the books differ: Bailey and Love 28e treats by rest and aspiration, while SRB does a subtotal excision for a thick sac or a chylocele. I would follow SRB and excise." That tumour clause is the one examiners wait for, and naming the filarial disagreement is what shows you have read the tropical section rather than the general one. B&L gives the reason behind the tumour clause: "if a tumour is suspected, the hydrocele should not be punctured (risk of malignant needle-track implantation)."​B&L 86 · p.1564

5Rapid-fire viva

Define a hydrocele and give its types.

An abnormal collection of serous fluid in part of the processus vaginalis, usually the tunica vaginalis around the testis and occasionally along the spermatic cord.​B&L 86 · p.1564 Structurally: communicating or congenital, where a patent processus lets peritoneal fluid into the scrotum and which is associated with indirect inguinal hernia; and non-communicating or vaginal, where the processus is closed and fluid accumulates from excessive production or defective absorption. Anatomically SRB gives four: vaginal, infantile reaching the internal ring, congenital reaching the peritoneum at the internal ring, and encysted hydrocele of the cord.​SRB 26 · p.1057 And clinically, primary or idiopathic versus secondary to epididymal or testicular disease.

How do you distinguish a hydrocele from an inguinoscrotal hernia?

You can get above a hydrocele, feeling only normal cord above it, because it is a purely scrotal swelling; you cannot get above an inguinoscrotal hernia, which is continuous with the inguinal canal and has no upper limit.​Das 38 · p.597–598 A hydrocele also transilluminates and has no cough impulse and is not reducible.

Why must every adult hydrocele have an ultrasound?

Because a hydrocele may be secondary to epididymal or testicular disease,​B&L 86 · p.1564 and in a tense hydrocele you cannot palpate the testis to exclude a tumour. A testicular tumour can present as a hydrocele, so the ultrasound is examining the testis, not the fluid. If the testis is abnormal, take tumour markers before any intervention.

Which is more likely to be hiding a tumour: a big tense hydrocele or a small lax one?

The small lax one. A large tense primary hydrocele is usually idiopathic; a secondary hydrocele is typically small and lax, so the testis remains palpable and the underlying disease can be felt. Either way the ultrasound decides, because palpation of a testis through fluid is unreliable.

Describe the hydrocele fluid.

Amber-coloured, specific gravity 1.022 to 1.024, containing water, salts, albumin and fibrinogen, and often cholesterol and tyrosine crystals. It does not clot by itself, but if blood enters it the fibrinogen is activated and it clots firmly.​SRB 26 · p.1057 That is why repeated or traumatic aspiration leaves a thickened loculated sac that is harder to operate on later.

Why do most congenital hydroceles need no operation?

Because more than 80% of newborn boys have a patent processus vaginalis and most close spontaneously, closure beginning in late gestation and continuing through infancy and childhood.​B&L 86 · p.1564 So observe in infancy, and operate if it persists beyond about two years or if there is an associated hernia, through the groin with ligation of the patent processus.

What are the operations for an adult hydrocele, and what decides between them?

Bailey and Love gives three: plication (Lord's operation), suitable when the sac is reasonably thin walled, bunching the sac with sutures and minimal dissection; eversion, with the testis placed in a pouch dissected in the fascial planes of the scrotum; and aspiration.​B&L 86 · p.1565 SRB gives five, adding subtotal excision of the sac for a thick sac or chylocele, and splitting eversion into Jaboulay's (partial excision then eversion) and Sharma and Jhawer's (the scrotal pouch).​SRB 26 · p.1059 The thickness of the sac decides: thin sac, plicate; thick sac, evert or partly excise. Excision is only ever subtotal, because the tunica is reflected onto the cord and epididymis and taking it out whole would mean orchidectomy.​SRB 26 · p.1060

Would you aspirate a hydrocele?

Not as definitive treatment: it recurs, and the fluid clots if blood enters it, leaving a thickened sac.​SRB 26 · p.1057 It has a place as palliation in a patient unfit for surgery. And never aspirate before excluding a testicular tumour on ultrasound, because a scrotal needle or incision in the presence of a tumour risks local spread and changes the surgical approach.

Hydrocele or epididymal cyst?

In a vaginal hydrocele the fluid surrounds the testis so the testis cannot be felt separately; in an epididymal cyst the testis is palpable separately, below and in front of the cyst. Both transilluminate and both are fluctuant and both allow you to get above them. SRB groups the scrotal differentials together: haematocele, pyocele, cyst of epididymis, spermatocele and varicocele, alongside primary and secondary vaginal hydrocele.​SRB 26 · p.1056

What causes a secondary hydrocele?

Epididymal or testicular disease.​B&L 86 · p.1564 In practice: acute or tuberculous epididymo-orchitis, testicular tumour, trauma, torsion and filariasis. In India, filariasis first: B&L says "filarial hydroceles and chyloceles account for up to 80% of hydroceles in tropical countries, where the parasite Wuchereria bancrofti is endemic", following "repeated attacks of filarial epididymo-orchitis".​B&L 86 · p.1566 Treat the cause, not just the fluid.

What happens if a hydrocele does not transilluminate?

Reconsider the diagnosis. Failure to transilluminate suggests a thick-walled or calcified sac, blood (haematocele), pus (pyocele), or a solid swelling such as a tumour or a chronic inflammatory mass. Get an ultrasound.

Sources. S Das. A Manual on Clinical Surgery 13e (2018); Bailey & Love's Short Practice of Surgery 28e; SRB's Manual of Surgery 6e. Citations give chapter and printed page. In the 28th edition of Bailey & Love, the testis and scrotum are chapter 86. The two books agree substantively here; SRB's four anatomical types and its description of the fluid are the Indian exam framework, and the sac-thickness rule is Bailey & Love's. The two books do not agree on what Jaboulay's operation is, or on whether aspiration has any place; both disagreements are set out in the amber boxes.
